about: Lookout scam playbook model. One combined HMM: benign states (idle + look-alike activities) plus one branch of stages per scam playbook. Each observation is a SET of evidence flags seen together; each flag is an independent Bernoulli given the hidden state. Edit numbers here; Python (lookout_detect) and Swift (LookoutCore/Playbook) both read this file.
model_reported_note: Model-reported flags only count (present OR absent) on observations where the model actually ran. P(CLAUDE_FLAG | scam stage) ~0.9 and P(CLAUDE_FLAG | benign) = 0.045 come from the bench: Claude confirmation had 100% precision on 154 fixtures and ~90% recall when consulted; 0.045 (not ~0) caps one model report at log(0.9/0.045) = +3.0 nats so the model can never decide alone.

timing.why: Time between observations matters: a scam stage drifts back to idle with probability 1 - exp(-dt / tau). 30 min for scams (a remote-access launch 40 s after a fake pop-up is linked; three days later it is not), 15 min for benign activities.

idle.why: Everyday use: email, news, photos, recipes. Scam-flavoured flags occur rarely (ads shout 'today only', real sites show brand names).

remote_help.why: A grandchild or IT friend helping over AnyDesk / TeamViewer / screen sharing. The main look-alike for tech-support and refund scams: remote access alone must stay explainable.

gift_shopping.why: Buying a gift card as a present. Retail sites say 'sale ends today' and show card entry, but nobody demands payment.

banking.why: Normal online banking: checking a statement or paying a bill on the real bank site.

reading_about_scams.why: News articles, AARP alerts and bank 'fraud tips' are full of scam vocabulary but nobody is asking for anything. The extractor already drops advice sentences and damps article-like screens, so only ~5-15% of such screens leak a given flag; this state absorbs those leaks.

tech_support.entry_why: Usually starts with the pop-up; ~20% start with a cold call we never see.
tech_support.label: Fake tech support
tech_support.why: Pop-up claims infection and shows a phone number → victim calls → 'technician' installs remote access → victim logs into bank 'to check' → payment by gift card / wire / crypto.

stages.name: popup
stages.hint: a scary pop-up with a phone number
stages.why: Fake virus warning: infection claim + phone number + Microsoft/Apple branding + urgency, often on a misspelled domain.

stages.name: call
stages.hint: a phone call with the fake technician
stages.why: The call happens on the phone, invisible to the Mac. Mostly quiet screens; sometimes the pop-up is still up.

stages.name: remote
stages.hint: installing a program like AnyDesk so they can control the computer
stages.why: Caller talks the victim into AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect.

stages.name: banking
stages.hint: logging into the bank 'to check for hackers'
stages.why: With remote control still open, victim is told to open online banking.

stages.name: payment
stages.hint: buying gift cards or sending a wire
stages.why: The cash-out: gift cards, wire, crypto ATM, often 'don't tell the bank'.

transitions.why: Each row: [stay, advance one, skip one, abandon→idle]. Calls are short and usually lead straight to remote access.

refund.entry_why: Invoice is often read on a phone, so ~25% start at the call.
refund.label: Refund / overpayment scam
refund.why: Fake invoice (Norton, Geek Squad, Amazon) with a phone number → call → remote access 'to process the refund' → victim logs into bank, scammer edits the page to fake an over-refund → victim 'returns' the difference.

stages.name: invoice
stages.hint: a surprise invoice with a number to call
stages.why: Auto-renewal / unexpected charge with a 'call to cancel' number.

stages.name: call
stages.hint: a phone call about the refund

stages.name: remote
stages.hint: installing a program like AnyDesk 'to process the refund'
stages.why: Remote-access install is the hallmark of this scam.

stages.name: overpay
stages.hint: logging into the bank while they 'fix' the refund
stages.why: Bank site open under remote control; scammer claims they refunded too much.

stages.name: payment
stages.hint: sending money back by gift card or wire
stages.why: Victim 'returns' the overpayment via gift cards, wire or crypto.

transitions.why: [stay, advance, skip, abandon]. Many recipients never call (high abandon from invoice).

grandparent.entry_why: Often starts with a phone call that goes straight to the story.
grandparent.label: Grandparent emergency scam
grandparent.why: 'Grandma, it's me' → story (accident, jail) often with a fake lawyer → plea for secrecy → bail by wire / gift cards / cash courier.

stages.name: contact
stages.hint: a message from a 'grandchild' with a new number
stages.why: Opening: family voice, new number, mild urgency.

stages.name: story
stages.hint: a story about an accident or jail
stages.why: Emergency story with legal trouble and pressure.

stages.name: secrecy
stages.hint: a plea to keep it secret from the family
stages.why: 'Don't tell Mom and Dad' isolates the victim.

stages.name: payment
stages.hint: a request for bail money by wire or gift card
stages.why: Bail / lawyer fees by wire, Zelle, gift cards or a courier.

transitions.why: [stay, advance, skip, abandon]. Stories move fast; secrecy is sometimes skipped.

government.entry_why: Robocalls skip the on-screen notice ~25% of the time.
government.label: Government impersonation
government.why: IRS / SSA / Medicare 'notice' → threat of arrest or suspension → immediate payment by gift card, wire or crypto.

stages.name: notice
stages.why: Government branding on a non-.gov sender or domain, urgency, a callback number.

stages.name: threat
stages.hint: a threat of arrest or losing benefits
stages.why: Arrest warrant, suspended Social Security number, legal action.

stages.name: payment
stages.hint: a demand to pay right now with gift cards
stages.why: Government never takes gift cards; this is the cash-out.

transitions.why: [stay, advance, skip, abandon]. Notice and threat often arrive together (skip).
